newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt accuses opposition over budget.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt accuses opposition over budget.

text.p: Czech Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik accused the opposition Social Democrats on Tuesday of endangering the country's international financial reputation by demanding changes to the state budget.

But the Social Democrats, who hold the balance of power after inconclusive elections, said they were only seeking reasonable parliamentary control over the process and forecast that a balanced budget would pass on schedule in December.
Under conservative Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, the Czech Republic has been lauded as the economic success story of the former Eastern Bloc.
But the record of stability has come into question since Klaus lost his parliamentary majority, the fall in inflation ground to a halt, and the trade deficit soared.
Shortly before the debate on the 1997 budget began on Tuesday, the Social Democrats said they would demand two changes to the draft.

Kocarnik, himself under heavy fire for his handling of a recent banking crisis, said: "The overall economic situation in the Czech Republic is very good and (the country) is economically and politically stable. The confidence of foreign investors and the inflow of money from abroad is based on this."
Meddling with the budget would be grave, he said. "Sending this signal would mean sending the wrong signal: that it is not safe to put money...into the Czech Republic."
The Czech Republic needs foreign capital to cover a trade deficit which soared over 100 billion crowns ($3.7 billion) in the first eight months of this year, about the same as for the whole of 1995.
Its record of stability has attracted foreign investment but there have been signs that the inflow has slowed recently.

Stanislav Gross, the Social Democrats' leader in parliament, played down the significance of what his party wanted and, speaking before the first reading of the draft budget began, said he still saw the law being passed by the end of the year.

He also said his party would not seek any change to the overall levels of expenditure and revenue, which will be balanced as in the past four years. It wanted only changes to two paragraphs in the government's draft budget.

The first allows the government to change the budget after parliament has approved it as long as this does not affect overall revenue and expenditure. The second gives powers to the mayors of major Czech cities to change their municipal budgets.
The Klaus government has been weakened since it lost its parliamentary majority in elections at the end of May.

His coalition holds only 99 seats in the 200-seat chamber. The Social Democrats can therefore block the budget if they win full support from the two other opposition parties, the Communists and the far-right Republicans.
Analysts have said the budget will mark the first major policy showdown between the government and opposition, and could trigger early elections possibly next spring.
The budget is based on a forecast of economic growth of between 4.7 and 5.3 percent, and 8.6 percent inflation.
